summary: One Fire, Many Worlds is an interactive web dashboard that turns NASA's microgravity combustion data into fire safety answers for the places where people will live: spacecraft and stations, a Moon base and rover, a spacesuit, a Mars habitat, and Earth. It organizes 2,199 individual tests from 25 investigations in NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository by oxygen, pressure, fuel and outcome, and ranks the investigations for each world across NASA's three fire safety fronts: prevention, detection and suppression. Users can compare investigations side by side, open a profile for each material, check what was tested near a given atmosphere, download the cleaned test table, and ask questions in plain language to an AI assistant that cites the PSI record behind every statement. The dashboard also shows what has not been tested yet, such as fabrics and plastics in Moon-base air, so researchers can see where the next experiments are needed. Every figure traces back to its source.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

One Fire, Many Worlds reads NASA's PSI combustion data as one question asked in five places: will it burn here, will we notice, and can we put it out? Each world (Station and spacecraft, Moon base and rover, Spacesuit, Mars habitat, Earth) has its own page with its atmosphere, a chart of oxygen against pressure for every test, the investigations ranked by relevance on each fire safety front, and a clear statement of what PSI holds and what it does not.

HOW IT WORKS

- Investigations: 25 PSI investigations with objectives, fuels, sample shape and size, test conditions, variables and measurements, and a side-by-side comparison of up to three.

- Materials: a profile for each of 10 materials with its tests, smoke data and open questions.

- Will it burn?: pick an oxygen level and pressure and see the tests run near that condition and how they ended.

- Data: all 2,199 tests, filterable and downloadable as CSV for predictive modeling.

- Timeline: from accidents (Apollo 1, Apollo 13, Mir) to the experiments that followed.

- Ask the data: an AI assistant answers questions and writes short research reports using only the site's data, citing the PSI record, test or document page behind each statement, and saying so when something is not in the data.

- Sources and figures: every cited page and figure opens with its exact passage and a link to the NASA document.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Professors, students and aerospace engineers can find, compare and interpret decades of combustion results in minutes. The site states PSI data first and marks anything from outside PSI separately. It highlights gaps, for example no solid material in PSI was burned in Moon-base air, to help plan future experiments. An Earth page links the research to smoke detection, water-mist extinguishers and firefighter gear.

TOOLS

HTML, CSS and JavaScript without a framework; three.js for the 3D models of each world; Python for downloading, cleaning and verifying the PSI tables; a Node.js serverless function on Vercel for the AI assistant (Anthropic Claude). A script checks the site's key figures against the data.

CREATIVITY AND TEAM FACTORS

Instead of listing investigations, we organized the evidence by the worlds where crews will live and by gravity, so the gaps become visible. We decided that nothing is invented: every number traces to a PSI record or a NASA document page. The interface is available in English and Spanish.
